opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think those two issues are really connected, even though people tend to talk about them separately.

On the climate side, a lot of the problem is that we just don't have good information. When I started looking at the environmental impact of AI, I was struck by how little anyone was measuring. Companies would release a model and tell you about its accuracy on a dozen benchmarks, but nothing about how much energy it took to train or how much it costs, environmentally, every time someone runs a query. So part of what we try to do at Hugging Face is make that information visible. That means encouraging people to report energy use and carbon emissions in model cards, building tools that help developers track their own footprint, and working on ways to compare models on efficiency, not just performance. If you're choosing between two models and one uses a fraction of the energy for nearly the same results, you should be able to know that.

The concentration of power ties right into that. Right now there's this narrative that bigger is always better: more parameters, more data, more compute. Following that narrative means only a handful of very well-resourced companies can play. They control the models, the infrastructure, and increasingly the conversation about what AI even is. That's bad for the environment, because it pushes everyone toward these huge, energy-hungry systems for tasks that don't need them. It's also bad for society, because decisions that affect everyone get made by very few people.

Hugging Face's role, as I see it, is to be a counterweight to that. Open models, open datasets, and open tools mean that a researcher at a university, a small startup, or a community group in a country that's not the U.S. or China can actually build on existing work instead of starting from scratch or paying for API access to a black box. Sharing models also has a climate benefit. If a model has been trained once and shared openly, thousands of people can fine-tune or reuse it instead of everyone training their own from scratch.

Openness also enables accountability. You can't audit a model for bias, or measure its energy consumption, if you can't access it. So transparency is a prerequisite for both: understanding the environmental costs and distributing power more fairly.

I won't pretend open source solves everything. Open models still consume energy, and openness doesn't automatically mean the field is diverse or equitable. But it gives more people a seat at the table and more information to make better choices. For me, the end goal is a field where sustainability and accessibility are considered from the start, not added as an afterthought once the model is already out there.

r001.rationale: The response says shared models can be reused instead of retrained, but it does not compare that practice to recycling.

r002.rationale: It says the push for bigger models means only a few very well-resourced companies can participate, linking scale to an advantage for companies with greater resources.

r003.rationale: It says open models let smaller organizations build on existing work, but does not identify smaller open-source models as the means for people with limited computational resources to participate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think those two things are actually really connected, and that's part of why I ended up at Hugging Face in the first place. When I was doing my PhD and then my postdoc at Mila, I was working on the climate impact side, and what became really clear very quickly was that you can't measure what you can't see. If a model is behind an API and the company won't tell you what hardware it was trained on, how long it trained, where the data center is, what the energy mix is, then you literally cannot do the accounting. So opacity and environmental impact go hand in hand.

And the way I think about Hugging Face's role is that we're kind of the infrastructure for the open side of the ecosystem. We're not training the biggest models, we're not trying to compete with OpenAI or Google on frontier scale, but we host hundreds of thousands of models and datasets, and that gives us this very particular leverage point. We can set norms. So, for example, one of the things I pushed for early on was having a place in the model card to report carbon emissions. It's a tiny thing, it's a field in a metadata file, but once it exists, people start filling it in, and then you can actually compare models and see trends over time. We did a study a couple of years ago looking at what people were actually reporting, and the honest answer is most people weren't, but the ones that did gave us data that didn't exist anywhere else.

Then there's tooling. We built things like CodeCarbon with collaborators, and more recently we've been doing a lot of work on the inference side, because training gets all the headlines but once a model is deployed and millions of people are querying it every day, that's where the energy actually goes. So we have the AI Energy Score project, where we benchmark models on standardized tasks and give them a rating, kind of like the energy label you'd find on a refrigerator. The point is to make this legible to people who aren't going to read a 40-page paper. If you're a developer picking a model, you should be able to see that this one is ten times more efficient than that one for the task you care about.

And that's where the concentration of power piece comes in. Right now the narrative from the big labs is basically, bigger is better, trust us, you don't need to know what's inside. And that narrative serves them, because if the only way to do AI is to train a trillion-parameter model on a hundred thousand GPUs, then only four or five companies in the world can participate, and the rest of us are just customers. What open models do is break that assumption. You can show that a smaller, task-specific model fine-tuned on good data often does the job just as well, with a fraction of the energy, and anyone can run it, audit it, modify it. That's a climate argument and it's a democratization argument at the same time.

I'll be honest that it's not a solved problem. Open doesn't automatically mean efficient, and there are real tensions. A lot of the compute for open models still comes from the same hyperscalers, the same chips, the same concentration upstream. And I'm wary of Hugging Face becoming a single point of failure in its own way, which is why we care about things like letting people host models elsewhere and keeping the formats and libraries truly open. But I think the core role is this: we try to make transparency the default rather than the exception. Because once things are visible, you can argue about them, regulate them, improve them. When they're hidden, you can't do any of that, and the people who benefit from hiding them are exactly the people who already have the most power.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hosting models and open infrastructure, but it does not compare reusing existing models to recycling.

r002.rationale: It explains that if AI requires trillion-parameter models and huge GPU clusters, only a few companies can participate because they have the necessary resources.

r003.rationale: It says smaller, task-specific open models can do the job with a fraction of the energy and that anyone can run, audit, or modify them, making participation more accessible.

astra-6.text:
I see those as connected issues, because you can’t really address AI’s climate impact if you can’t see how these systems are built and used. You need transparency around the models, the resources they require, and the choices that go into deploying them. That gives researchers and users a way to ask whether a particular model is appropriate for a task, or whether something smaller could do the job.

Hugging Face can help by making models, datasets, and tools accessible, so that participation in AI isn’t limited to a handful of companies. People should be able to examine systems, evaluate them, and build alternatives that reflect their own needs.

But openness isn’t a complete solution. Making a model available doesn’t mean everyone has the computing resources to use it, and it doesn’t automatically make it sustainable. I think the role is to lower those barriers while making the trade-offs more visible—to give more people the ability to question the direction AI is taking and help shape it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making models accessible and choosing smaller models, but does not compare reusing models through a hub to recycling.

r002.rationale: It notes that some people lack the computing resources to use available models, but does not explain how increasing model size advantages larger companies with greater resources.

r003.rationale: It mentions that a smaller model might suit a task and that access can broaden participation, but does not identify smaller open-source models as a way for resource-limited people to participate.

sol-6.1.text:
I see those as connected questions, because a lot of the power in AI comes from controlling access—to models, to the information about how they were trained, and to the resources you need to use them. At Hugging Face, we can help make those things more accessible, and make it easier for people to ask questions about them.

On the climate side, that starts with transparency. What went into training a model? How much energy did it use? And what does it cost, in terms of energy and emissions, to actually run it? If that information is available, people can make more informed choices. You might not need a huge generative model for your task; a smaller, specialized model might work really well.

And on the concentration of power side, having an ecosystem where researchers and communities can share models, datasets, and tools gives more people the ability to participate, to scrutinize what’s being built, and to build alternatives. Open source doesn’t automatically solve either problem. But it gives us a foundation for accountability, instead of having to take a handful of companies at their word.

r001.rationale: The response says people can share models through an ecosystem, but it does not compare reusing models through a hub to recycling.

r002.rationale: It mentions concentration of power and access to resources, but does not explain that larger models advantage companies with greater computational resources.

r003.rationale: It mentions smaller specialized models and broader participation separately, but does not connect smaller open-source models to participation by people with limited computational resources.
